title: Pick people that are not in a conflict of interest
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Who sits at your table, and do they want you to grow?

groups.heading: He sees the potential, not the present

lines.text: As I retell it, the author bought a small film company that others called a maker of cheap movies. I read a line.
I knew that if I could increase their budgets it would allow them to make bigger films

He defended himself, I said: we make movies that are profitable. That film company became a massive success. He sees what a company can be in the future. He doesn't see it in its present state. He visualizes. He builds a relationship with these people and makes them feel good about growth.

groups.heading: Pick people that are not in a conflict of interest

lines.text: What about the board of directors, I asked? There is a conflict of interest. Some of the people on his board own content companies too, and they don't like that he keeps buying content. They are in direct competition.

They are jealous and envious that he is buying companies and growing, I said, and their company isn't growing as fast. That is a mistake the author made, bringing them onto the board. Thank God he had enough shares to balance it.

If you are building a board for your company, I said, you have to pick people who are not going to be a conflict of interest. People who are strategically interested in your growth. Otherwise you are going to have a big problem.

groups.heading: A Lone Ranger is a red flag

lines.text: Big lessons, I said. Number one: when you build a board, pick strategic partners without conflicts of interest, without big egos, people who are nurturing and genuinely interested in your company's growth.

Number two: when you do deals, make sure the person is relationship-oriented, not win-lose. Find out their style from what they have done in the past. Are they win-win, or short-term viewers? Do they have partners, or have they never had partners? Maybe they are a Lone Ranger. That is a red flag. They may say they want a partnership, but they will do it alone, and sooner or later they will come and get you.

Also expose yourself, I said: I'm a long-term player, here's why, here's how I see things. They will appreciate your demeanor. He builds trust right away. Building trust: that is what we learned from this chapter.
What does the history of your next partner tell you?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write who sits on your board or advises you.
Write whether any of them could be in conflict with your growth.
Write a deal partner's history: have they had partners?
Write the style you will look for: win-win or short-term.
Write what you will say to build trust in the first meeting.

check.q: What did I say a board member with a competing company is?
What did I say is a red flag in a partner?
What did I say you should do about your own style?
choices: Expose it: say you are a long-term player and why

recap: Pick strategic people without conflicts, check their history, and build trust.
